blocks.text: III. The third passage about the cock is 2 Reg. XVII, 30., where, of the peoples transferred by Shalmaneser from Assyria into Judaea, the Babylonians are said to have worshipped סכות־בנות Succoth-Benoth, and the Cuthaeans Nergal. Succoth-Benoth, that is, the hen with her chicks; and Nergal, that is, the cock, as the Hebrews would have it. For so the Talmudists in Sanhedrin, chapter 7, folio 63b: אנשי בבל עשו את סכות־בנות ומאי ניהו תרנגולת אנשי כותה עשו נרגל ומאי ניהו תרנגול, The men of Babel made [II, 679] Succoth-Benoth. What (idol) was this? A hen. The men of Cutha made Nergal. What was that? A cock. Solomon Jarchi: סכות־בנות דמות תרנגולת עם אפרוחיה נרגל דמות תרנגול, Succoth-Benoth was the image of a hen with her chicks, and Nergal the image of a cock. Kimchi: ובדברי רז״ל סכות־בנות זה תרנגולת היו עובדים והיה שמה סכות בנות וכמו שקורין לתרנגול סכוי כן היו [col. 113] קורין לתרנגולת סכות ובנות פירוש עם אפרוחיה נרגל זה תרנגולת הבר, In the words of our masters of blessed memory, Succoth-benoth is the hen, which they worshipped under this name. For just as they called the cock שכוי secui, so they called the hen סכות succoth. And the added benoth signifies that she was with her chicks. And nergal is the wild hen. The most trifling of trifles. Literally, סכות בנות Succoth-benoth are tents of daughters, or of girls. So when the Babylonians are said to have made Succoth-benoth, I understand that they built a shrine of goddesses who were called בנות benoth, that is, girls, just as the Greeks called Proserpina κόρην [korēn], that is, girl. So in Amos V, 26. סכות מלככם, the tabernacle of your king, that is, the shrine of your idol ^{(1)}. And what נרגל Nergal is, I do not know, except that almost the same name as this idol belongs to a species of palm called even today by the Persians, Arabs and Indians نارجيل [nārjīl] nergil, of which they tell wonders. It must therefore be considered whether the idol of the Persians could have been named from this palm, as in Syria ܪܡܘܢ Rimmon was from pomegranates, 2 Reg. V, 18.

IV. The fourth passage is Iob. III, 7. There, for the words of Job in which he curses the night in which he was born, Let no רננה, song, come in it, the Chaldee has: לא תעול רננא דתרנגול ברא למקלסה בה, Let not the song of the wild cock come to give praise in it. This does not concern the cock in general, but a fabulous cock of prodigious size, which we shall treat in the treatise On the Ostrich. And the same translator says more about it in the passages that follow, taken from Job and the Psalms.
